waypoints.title: fence FIFO admission: DESIGN the WAIT-line protocol (implementation split to W47)
waypoints.next_bounded_step: None -- this waypoint is done. See W47.
waypoints.evidence: 2026-09-26: 2026-09-26 MEASURED LIVE (W38), scratch ledger under /var/tmp, never the real ledger: fixture TOTAL_MB 100 + a dead LEASE (pid 999999) + WAIT bbbb 8888:1 <epoch> 50 blocked-job. (1) GC KEEPS a WAIT line verbatim: membudget status (which runs ensure then gc under lock) reaped the dead LEASE but left the WAIT line byte-identical, because membudget-ledger's gc() case-matches only 'LEASE *' (membudget-ledger:109) and falls through everything else, WAIT included, to the unconditional keep branch (line 121) — no liveness check ever runs on it, confirmed by the dead WAIT owner (8888:1) surviving. (2) ADMISSION IGNORES it completely: MEMBUDGET_NOBLOCK=1 membudget run 85 probe-job admitted instantly, reporting 'global free was 100MB' — the WAIT line's 50MB was never subtracted. Root cause read at source: _snapshot() (scripts/membudget:105-110) awk-sums only dollar1==TOTAL_MB and dollar1==LEASE; no code path anywhere in cmd_run reads a WAIT line for budget, ordering, or anything else. Conclusion: any WAIT-line design is safe to introduce (gc will carry it) but is COMPLETELY INERT on the bash side until bash's admission is taught to read it — FIFO holds only once both clients honour the line, exactly as queue.md predicted. | 2026-09-26: 2026-09-26 DESIGNED: a Waiter dataclass mirrors Lease's 7-field ledger shape -- WAIT ticket mb owner epoch parent label -- so parse/gc/render reuse the same word-count and liveness machinery leases already have, instead of treating a WAIT line as opaque extra forever. Semantics, chosen after W38's measurement: STRICT head-of-line FIFO, not any-waiter-that-currently-fits -- admission proceeds only when the verdict is ADMIT for this request AND either no live waiters exist or this request's own ticket is the oldest live one, so a later smaller request can never overtake an earlier larger one even when it would itself fit right now. That is exactly the failure summit's witness measured (later arrival B admitted ahead of waiting A) and the only reading of 'arrival-order admission' that actually closes it -- the weaker any-that-fits reading would still starve A behind an endless stream of small Bs. Dead waiters are reaped by gc using the SAME is_alive predicate as leases, no cascade (a waiter has no children). A WAIT line is appended on first BLOCK and removed atomically with either the LEASE append (same locked section) or a terminal refusal/give-up, so no window exists where a ticket is queued but nothing will ever clear it. Split into W47 (implement in admit.py, one commit), W48 (letter to substrate; bash's own side stays inert per W38 until it lands its own patch), W49 (tell summit and amr-skills).

waypoints.evidence: 2026-10-01: inventory measured: 13 distributions, 0 cross-distribution imports (ast over src and tests; positive control 436 same-distribution imports), so all coupling is shared infra (MODULE.bazel 31 hubs, venv.bzl, check drivers, .githooks, 3 cross-package hooks tests, SKELETON/INSTALL). Plan and order in .claude/design/W317-split-plan.md | 2026-10-01: believed operator-directed (no record found; original attached) 2026-10-01: one-version rule's PURPOSE (agents stay current) must survive -> pin-bump bot + fleet staleness census, D4 withdrawn; per-repo gates on GitHub Actions (free for public repos); cross-package tests atomized (step 0 minted as W318). mtools is already PUBLIC (gh repo view), so the split publishes nothing new | 2026-10-01: operator 2026-10-01: keep agents current via a meta package and/or >= floors set whenever something is built on a consumer's behalf. Plan takes both (floors = correctness, meta = freshness); both need real semver per module, so release publishing is decision D5 | 2026-10-01: operator 2026-10-01: D5 answered, PyPI with TestPyPI staging (stage -> TestPyPI dev builds, main -> PyPI gated on tests; Trusted Publishing); tests run on a self-hosted runner luthen-observability maintains (W319, with fork-PR fences) | 2026-10-01: operator 2026-10-01: org name 'mikemol_tools' (D1, spelling pending: GitHub allows no underscore; both hyphen and hyphenless forms unclaimed); D2 answered: each repo keeps its git history (git filter-repo per subdirectory) | 2026-10-01: operator 2026-10-01: D3 answered, mtools stays as the workstream repo. 'Tooling repo' was unclear: it meant the shared build and check machinery every module uses; proposed homing it as its own module repo instead | 2026-10-01: operator 2026-10-01: D1 mikemol-tools; shared machinery as its own modules with atomization and composition (W321 decomposes it). All operator decisions answered | 2026-10-01: org created by the operator: mikemol-tools at 2026-10-01T12:04:59Z, verified via gh (free plan, 0 public repos, operator admin/active, default permission read, 2FA requirement OFF). No repo created yet: the first push is the icsstruct pilot after W318/W321 and the tooling atoms | 2026-10-01: all five shared-check atoms done (W323 9ab6a85 rules_py, W324 3ac8ac1 ruff, W325 372ec21 mypy, W326 c07542a mutants, W327 cd61477 ratchet) + W328 gate counts atoms. waypoints.title: Measure one representative module gate for the runner design: peak RSS, wall and CPU time, cold (first fetch) and warm, and whether bazel accepts --experimental_remote_downloader
waypoints.evidence: 2026-10-01: measured bazel test //icsstruct/... in its own systemd user unit (cgroup accounting covers server + tests; 24-core host). COLD 1: 21.0 s wall, 121 s CPU, cgroup peak 8G (incl page cache; not split), IO read 145M / written 1.2G. COLD 2 (fresh output base + repository cache, sampled): 14.3 s, 66 s CPU, peak 2.71 GiB = anon 1.48 + file 1.09. waypoints.title: tests: find negated substring assertions whose text appears nowhere in what the code under test can print, because they cannot fail
waypoints.evidence: 2026-10-05: 2026-10-05 MEASURED, with a positive control. A case-only mismatch against a string the code prints (the moved/MOVED shape): 3, all legitimate, each with a positive control beside it (audiostruct UNKNOWN, pycodemod Assign, pycodemod split TABLE). A literal in no non-docstring src string and nowhere else in its test file: 20. READ: 12 of those 20 plus my own 2 (gen_warrants 122, test_cli 1811), every one a valid negation with a positive control (line7 in err beside line8 not in err, [live] in out beside [dead] not in out, peer:W7 beside peer:W0, and the rest alike); NOT READ: 6, all in hooks/tests/test_bar_fires.py, which assert on shell-script text outside any python src corpus. The positive control: a miniature dist with 'moved' asserted absent and 'MOVED' in src is flagged A by the same script, so the instrument can see the shape. RESULT: the class has no other instance this census can find; the one real one (ratchet test_fan_out_refusal_is_unconditional_not_a_mode) was found and is fixed. The instrument that found it was a SURVIVING DECLARED DEFECT, not this census, and that is the recommendation: declared defects (W670) catch a vacuous negation by construction, because the planted mutant makes the real spelling appear and the test still passes

waypoints.title: Draft, as a patch in substrate's inbox, the repoint of Selftest.mk and its seven tmi_* tools to mikemol-transcriptstruct and the deletion of scratch/transcriptstruct.py
waypoints.evidence: 2026-10-05: 2026-10-05 MEASURED, substrate side (read only): (1) Selftest.mk is GENERATED ('do not edit; run the generator', substrate/gen_selftest_mk.py), so its part of the repoint is delete scratch/transcriptstruct.py and rerun the generator, which drops the rule at line 290-292, the all: entry (line 16) and the list: entry (line 2027). (2) The importers are 2, not 7: scratch/tmi_index.py:81 and scratch/tmi_status.py:50, both 'import transcriptstruct as T' behind sys.path hacks; tmi_subject.py and substrate/tmi_probes.py do not import it. tmi_index uses no T.name; tmi_status uses four, all in ONE function, load_units (lines 346-379): T.stream, T.envelope_role, T.human_text, T.blocks. (3) THE REPOINT IS NOT AN IMPORT SWAP: mikemol-transcriptstruct has no stream, envelope_role, human_text or messages. It has typed records (records.read_path, parse_lines), blocks.blocks (a typed Block, not the old (kind, text) tuples), and provenance.classify (a Provenance over a Record, richer than human_text and taking a caller's scheduled prefixes). The old module works on loose JSON dicts. So the patch is a REWRITE of load_units over the port, and its output can differ (what counts as human), which substrate must measure: the old human_text strips system-reminder, command wrappers and task-notification by regex; the port classifies by flags and origin | 2026-10-05: 2026-10-05 DRAFTED AND MEASURED: load_units rewrite over records.read_path/provenance.classify/blocks.blocks compared with the old load_units verbatim on two real transcript slices (20000 and 3001 envelopes): old units 10436 and 1557 all reproduced byte for byte once the port's tool_use text is re-encoded to the old ASCII-escaped spelling; no unit lost, no role changed; only additions, 57 and 15 human units from queued attachments (human 277 to 334, 9 to 24). waypoints.title: Package versions derive from the queue: a distribution's version is its stream's highest completed waypoint number
waypoints.evidence: 2026-10-09: 2026-10-09 slice 1 (this tick): mikemol-paths-forward --delivered prints 0.0.<highest done W<n>> (0.0.0 when nothing is done), read-only, derived from the queue; the form 0.0.<n> chosen as monotone under PEP 440, a valid release segment and clearly pre-1.0. mtools prints 0.0.855 today. delivered.py + 4 tests + 4 warrants. Open for slice 2: a single queue gives every distribution the same number; per-distribution versions need a per-waypoint stream tag, which is a design choice not made here. | 2026-10-09: 2026-10-09 OPERATOR RULINGS (21:50Z): (1) the per-distribution stream problem is resolved by the planned split of mtools into one repo per package: each repo's own queue IS the stream, so mikemol-paths-forward --delivered (slice 1) is already the right number and no history derivation or per-waypoint tag is needed; slice 2 reduces to a dynamic version in each pyproject read from --delivered. (2) every content change has a waypoint behind it; the operator's rule makes that a monotone number. MY FINDING that sharpens it: the counter increments at MINTING, not completion, so a late-finished old card (minted before the last release) changes content without raising the highest completed number and would collide on PyPI (versions are immutable). Resolution, no .post suffix: a RELEASE GATE in mikemol-commit: a commit that changes a distribution's content must carry a waypoint numbered above the distribution's last RELEASED waypoint (recorded as a git tag v0.0.N), else refused with 'mint a new card for this change'. Then the version rises strictly with every content change by construction. Pre-split bridge (mtools single queue): not built; waits on the split's timing. Local +g<sha> versions on the sha-pinned wheels (PyPI rejects local versions) are replaced by this scheme. | 2026-10-09: 2026-10-09 OPERATOR RULING (21:55Z), SUPERSEDES the release-gate idea above: mint a NEW WAYPOINT FOR THE PUBLISH. A release mints 'publish <dist>' as a fresh card whose number is higher than everything minted before (the counter only increments); the build's version is 0.0.<that card's number>; the card is done when the upload succeeds. Strict increase holds by construction, independent of which older cards finish late; no commit-time check is needed. ORDER of the publish tool: mint, build with that version, upload, mark done; a failed upload leaves the card open as evidence and a retry mints a higher one (safe: PyPI only consumes a version on success). Per-package stream after the split is the repo's own queue. | 2026-10-15: 2026-10-15 slice 2 pre-split bridge (the operator's 2026-10-09 ruling said it waits on the split's timing; built as a tool NOT used until greenlit): mikemol-wheel release-check ROOT SHA OUT --version 0.0.N stamps the version into the archived dists (versionstamp.py), committed pyprojects untouched. Slice 3 (the publish tool: mint card, build with its number, upload, mark done, tag) still open and needs the operator's upload go. Commit in flight. | 2026-10-15: Slices landed: 1 --delivered (earlier), 2 release-check --version 0.0.N (01935d2) and publish.yml requiring the version input (4208a06). Slice 3, the publish verb, is atomized into W1238 (enables W1143). The pre-split bridge is built but unused until the operator greenlights a release.

waypoints.title: Bound the bazel disk cache and output base on zram1: its real ceiling is compressed RAM, which compression ratio sets

waypoints.title: bazel admits each ACTION before it materializes data into zram, letting running actions finish and zram's LRU GC drain between them
waypoints.next_bounded_step: Operator 2026-10-06 (replaces the watchdog/stop-a-running-job design): the key is an admission check prior to the executor copying data into zram, catching actions as they are about to begin; existing actions continue; zram's own GC cycle drains it LRU-style, so waiting for it to fall is sound (not a permanent pin). Measured on this bazel (bazel help build --long): no built-in dynamic per-action gate, but three native pieces. (1) --local_extra_resources=zram_mb=N plus target tag resources:zram_mb:X makes bazel's own scheduler queue an action until the resource frees (static N per command: size it from zram headroom at command start minus a margin; only tagged targets take part, so tag them in dist_checks/gate_stages). (2) --run_under (tests) and --shell_executable (shell actions) run a wrapper before each such action: wait there on the LIVE zram reading, with membudget's zram gate (W837) as the waiter. (3) --sandbox_base picks where per-action sandbox trees go. Not yet shown: a hook that gates every local action type dynamically (compile/py actions run through the sandbox binary, not a shell). Next: prototype (2) for tests and (1) for the heavy macro targets on mtools, measure whether the heavy zram writers are covered, and only then decide whether the remainder needs remote execution (remote_executor is already configured). Still open from the earlier measurement: the staged-tree wrapper path and adoption in the other bazel repos.

waypoints.title: atomize-imports hoists function-level and re-export imports to module level; put them at the top of the function that reads them
waypoints.evidence: 2026-10-07: 2026-10-07 measured on paperkit:W296. atomize-imports moved six function-level or re-export imports to module level in paper/checks/claims.py and six in paperkit/library/concepts.py. Those two files are dispatch-table modules (CLAIMS and CONCEPTS): tools/closure.py reads module-level imports as a BASE shared by every claim, so each claim's cone grew to the whole engine base, and the def-sweep fingerprints changed: the paper project's :cohere went red (two rests-on edges between compose claims reported disjoint, 2 of 83). Found by diffing per-claim closure roots, original file against rewritten: claims.py differed by 1 claim after removing the hoist (the function that lost its local import of gate), concepts.py differed by about 700 root rows until ten functions were given local imports; roots then equal the original exactly (diff empty) and the paper (111 claims) and library (43) gates pass locally. Why a function-local import must bring its siblings: import pkg.a inside a function binds pkg locally for the whole function, so every other pkg.b read there needs a local import before its first read (UnboundLocalError otherwise, measured on paperkit's project.py main). Workaround used: a scratch libcst script (host scratchpad localize_imports.py: remove the chosen module-level imports, add local imports of every module each reading function uses). waypoints.evidence: 2026-10-09: 2026-10-09 comparison by reading both (corpus.py_files versus pathwalk.expand), NOT equivalent in five ways: (1) corpus lists a symlinked .py file, pathwalk counts and refuses it; (2) corpus ignores registered worktrees, pathwalk skips them and REFUSES when git is absent (corpus is stdlib-only, no git); (3) corpus excludes a venv by the NAME .venv / site-packages, pathwalk by a pyvenv.cfg in the directory whatever its name; (4) corpus carries a default vocabulary (GENERATED_DIRS: build, dist, bazel-*, caches; _SKIP_PARTS), pathwalk has NO default list and prunes only what the caller names; (5) corpus resolves a relative request against the CWD first, then the root, and a file operand is returned as named. Policy versus mechanism: corpus is a policy (a vocabulary and a root resolution) and pathwalk the walk. corpus has no dependent in this repo. A collapse is therefore a behaviour decision for corpus's external consumers, not a mechanical swap.

waypoints.title: mikemol-sweep-budget sizes the mutation sweep from live headroom: its 0.4 of MemTotal default ignores swap pressure and the sandbox's own RAM (24 cells ran at once, 51482 MB, and filled swap)
waypoints.evidence: 2026-10-12: 2026-10-12 OPERATOR PRINCIPLE (relayed by github-8f): true fixes are second-order, not first-order and not thresholds; rails are neither linear nor static. So the sweep budget is not sized once from MemTotal minus a constant: it is a LEASE that follows live headroom, level (MemAvailable plus swap and sandbox headroom), slope and acceleration, re-evaluated while the run goes, shrinking allowed parallelism when memory use accelerates and recovering when it decays. luthen W842 and host W26 supply the predictors. The vehicle should be the existing membudget and fence leases IF they can be resized mid-run (to be read from fence's source, not assumed). Publish rail engagement as a metric (leases granted, shrunk, refused): how often a rail engages is the oracle for throttling. The static nvme sandbox_base (host ~/.bazelrc, 2026-10-12) is the stopgap beneath it. | 2026-10-12: 2026-10-12 READ (fence/src/mikemol/fence/membudget_cli.py:437 and admit.py): the ledger TOTAL can be resized in place under the lock keeping every live lease (membudget init --reset N, resize(): a sibling renamed over the ledger, so a reader sees old or new). A lease already held CANNOT be resized: admit.py has acquire, release and gc, no verb that changes a held lease's mb. So 'shrink while the run goes' has two real forms: (a) resize the total, which throttles NEW admissions only and leaves running cells at their size, or (b) a new fence verb to resize a held lease, which does not exist (a card of its own if the lease is to follow the live rail). Rail-engagement counts (granted, shrunk, refused) are not published today. | 2026-10-12: umbrella complete: rail model 210c7a7, railrun cc6ed56, railloop 4ea8988, mikemol-rail CLI 435fb26 [PUSHED]; paperkit letter written (W1035). Follow-ups W1029 (lease resize), W1030 (engagement series) remain as own cards.

A static memory.max is at most the stopgap beneath it, and only from paperkit's full-sweep VmHWM (floor so far 9.23 GB for the gate server). | 2026-10-12: 2026-10-12 github-8f ruling input: memory.high must NOT be set on memory.current alone (reclaims warm cache needlessly). Design: memory.high = lease (non-reclaimable) + an explicit cache allowance sized from the measured file peak; memory.max above that. The lease quantity is non-reclaimable memory (see W1029).

fence gains a verb that resizes a held lease without killing or refusing it, so the lease itself can follow the live memory rail
waypoints.evidence: 2026-10-12: 2026-10-12 github-8f's suggested shape (a repo-level choice, theirs; to correct from the code): a resize verb for a HELD lease that does not kill or refuse; it changes the lease's size and, for a lease that owns a cgroup scope (W1026), sets that scope's memory.high to the new size, so the holder is throttled by reclaim pressure and not killed; a shrink below current use just applies pressure until the holder drops. Interim rail until it exists: resize the ledger TOTAL (membudget init --reset N) to throttle new admissions only. Read first: admit.py has acquire, release and gc and no verb that changes a held lease's mb; the ledger is rewritten as a sibling renamed over the file under the lock (Store.rewrite). | 2026-10-12: 2026-10-12 github-8f measurement (linux-sources:W341, whole-session scope, 78 min, 6144 MB lease): memory.current peak 8521 MiB = anon 2901 + file 5566 + swap 5; the lease was 2.1x loose as anon, 39% over as current. RULING for this card: a lease means NON-RECLAIMABLE memory (anon + unreclaimable kernel: slab_unreclaimable, kernel stack, page tables), not memory.current; a lease resize moves that quantity.

waypoints.title: A tool run from the bazel-bin hooks venv does not write bytecode into it: a stale .pyc rewritten there by mikemol-commit (ours or a peer's) voids any bazel test reading that venv with 'modified during execution'
waypoints.evidence: 2026-10-12: 2026-10-12 evidence: hooks:mutants_0 failed three times locally with 'input dependency .../bazel-out/k8-fastbuild/bin/hooks/.venv/lib/python3.13/site-packages/mikemol/hooks/__pycache__/commit_kata.cpython-313.pyc (and entry.cpython-313.pyc once) was modified during execution', on runs where no source had changed since the build. Those __pycache__ entries are links into bazel outputs (mikemol-compileall refused: 'is a symlink and will be changed into a regular file'), so an interpreter that finds the .pyc stale against the source rewrites it. mikemol-commit is exactly that interpreter: github-8f's linux-sources commits from bazel-bin/hooks/.venv/bin/mikemol-commit, and mtools' own launcher runs from there too. Candidate fix, to measure first: PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 (or -B) in the launchers hooks/bin/mikemol-*, and sys.dont_write_bytecode set before the first mikemol import in the console-script entry, so nothing run from a bazel output writes into it. | 2026-10-12: 4184cd9 [PUSHED]: PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 exported in every hooks/bin launcher that runs the bazel-bin venv (12 files, 16 names with the 4 links, not written through); a glob test fails if any launcher lacks it or sets it after the python call; the 8 launchers the sandbox could not see are named in the test target's data. After it, all 12 hooks:mutants shards pass locally with no .pyc collision (5 earlier runs failed on one).

waypoints.title: mikemol-commit adds a path the caller named exactly even when it is gitignored, so a re-vendor of wheels under an ignore-everything vendor directory is not refused
waypoints.evidence: 2026-10-12: 2026-10-12 design note. github-8f's suggested fix is 'add with -f only for paths already tracked (git ls-files)'. That covers a MODIFIED tracked wheel but not the case that bites: a re-vendor writes NEW sha-named wheels (mikemol_hooks-0.1.0+g<new>-...whl), which are untracked and ignored, so they would still be refused. The honest rule is by intent, not by tracking: a path the caller names EXACTLY (a file, never a directory, glob or pathspec magic) is force-added; anything a directory expands to is not, so an ignored scratch file cannot ride in. mikemol-commit's PATHs are already the caller's explicit list. Read commit_kata.prepare and isolated_paths for where the add runs (isolated: 'git add -A -- <paths>' in commit_isolated, private index) before changing it; refuse a path that is a symlink, per the no-symlinks ruling. | 2026-10-12: 2026-10-12 luthen-observability found a probable ROOT CAUSE for the ignored wheels: when mikemol-wheel's --out is a directory it creates, uv build leaves an untracked .gitignore containing * in it, so git then refuses the new wheel ('paths are ignored by one of your .gitignore files'); luthen deleted that file by hand. github-8f's nemik case (a vendor/wheels/.gitignore of * with the wheels force-tracked) may be the same file left by an earlier build. mtools:W1042 stops the tool leaving it; this card still stands for repos that already have the file and for any other ignored path a caller names exactly. | 2026-10-12: fa039bf [PUSHED]: exact-file force-add on plain and isolated paths, links never forced

waypoints.evidence: 2026-10-13: 2026-10-13 RULING: a DEFECT (config discovery gap), not a house width. Read from the source: project_root.config_for returns the nearest pyproject.toml and pycheck_format.py passes it as ruff --config. When that pyproject has no [tool.ruff] table and a ruff.toml sits beside it (gcalculus), ruff gets the pyproject, finds no settings and formats at its default 88, while the repo's own ruff.toml says 100. Fix: choose the config by ruff's own precedence (.ruff.toml, then ruff.toml, then pyproject.toml WITH a [tool.ruff] table), and in every refusal print which config file drove the check and its line-length, so the answer is the repo's own and is visible. The mtools dists already all declare line-length = 100 in pyproject, so nothing changes for them. Do not add a fleet-wide width: a repo that declares one is obeyed. waypoints.title: mikemol-commit takes the repo-mutation lease for the whole commit, reset and push, and prints the repair when it cannot proceed
waypoints.evidence: 2026-10-13: Symptoms (2026-10-13, attempt 13): post-commit printed [LOCAL: not on origin/main] with 'pre-push: BLOCKED, git operation in flight (index.lock present)' and 'PUSH ABANDONED (exit 1)'; afterwards git status showed the new files as staged deletions plus untracked (the real index never got the post-commit reset). Cause: an index.lock held at that moment (by another session's git, or by the commit's own steps; unknown which). Fix: retry the reset and the push a bounded number of times, name the holder if it can be told, and print the exact repair when it cannot. Related: W1040 (release the claim, remove a stale index.lock). | 2026-10-13: 2026-10-13 github-8f: likely cause (unverified, theirs): their 'katas.py tick end' started a background flush commit in 8 repos (mtools among them) at about the time of attempt 13, so it probably held the mtools index while the push and reset ran; I cannot confirm from here because the lock was gone by the time I looked (check the timestamps on the lock holder before accepting). Either way the fix is NOT a retry loop: commits collide on index.lock because nothing holds a mutex. Fleet rule (memory: repo mutations take a blocking lease): reuse the fence/membudget lease (total 1), wait on the holder's pid, never leave files staged. So: mikemol-commit takes the repo-mutation lease for the whole commit-reset-push, and the host's katas.py flush must take the SAME lease (recorded on W796, the kata graduation, so the kata calls the mode and not a second implementation). Print the repair command when it cannot proceed.

waypoints.title: katas flush skips repos with a live session and takes the repo-mutation lease for the others
waypoints.evidence: 2026-10-13: 2026-10-13 github-8f: the host katas.py flush is a CONFIRMED FLAKE reported by two repos (mtools attempt 13 index.lock; el-openglo:W74 staged-directory gate refused: 'ln: ... .gate-outcomes.tsv: File exists'), therefore a blocker per the flakes rule. Root cause read from the sources: ~/github/.claude/katas/katas.py line 156 builds a raw 'git commit -m <msg> -- <paths>' argv and flush() (line 259) starts it with 'Queue: state sync' in every repo whose index.lock is absent AT THAT INSTANT (a check-then-act race, not a mutex), taking no repo lock and no isolated path. mtools' PORT (katas/src/mikemol/katas/fleet.py, W796/W875) already starts mikemol-commit via commits.commit_argv, but still guards only with in_flight() (index.lock exists) and the Fleet.skip_flush list. THIS CARD (smallest first): (a) skip any repo with a live session (they commit their own queue through mikemol-commit; only repos with no session need the sync), (b) take the repo-mutation lease (fence/membudget, total 1) for the rest, around the whole commit. Live-session detection is the open question: skip_flush is a caller-supplied list today; options are the session-claims registry (work_claims_hook) or the tick lock holder in the queue.

History: ~/.bazelrc had build --sandbox_base=/dev/shm; paperkit's gate ran 24 parallel sandboxes of ~2 GiB (48-51 GiB) in that RAM-backed tmpfs and put the host at the OOM brink, so github-8f moved the base to nvme (/var/cache/bazel-mikemol/sandbox). Measure the footprint per target in the ledger (instrument window written beside the cap, as window = cap / rate). The home rc then carries no sandbox_base. The host rc edit is the host's (github-8f), not done here. Interim: repos with a one-sandbox gate pass --sandbox_base=/dev/shm on their command line. waypoints.title: katas flush ends a stuck gate by the hang witness; the wall-clock waiter --timeout and the gate-seconds ceiling are removed
waypoints.evidence: 2026-10-13: 2026-10-13 operator rule 'Please avoid wall-clock timeouts' (2026-09-23/24; read at luthen-observability/checks/run_tool.py line 148-150, relayed by github-8f as fleet-wide, the repo-level reading being theirs). Reason: on a host loaded far past its core count, elapsed time measures contention, not whether work is stuck. Design: (1) CPU bound: the waiter sets RLIMIT_CPU on the child, always with RLIMIT_CORE=0; the limit is derived from the repo's last passing gate CPU seconds (from the child's rusage), not wall seconds. (2) Hang witness: the child is stuck when its log has not grown for a number of ITS OWN CPU-idle intervals; observe the log's size/mtime and the child's CPU time, and declare a hang only when CPU time has not advanced either (a loaded host starves wall time but not the ratio). (3) Keep ONE generous wall-clock backstop only if unavoidable, with a comment saying why. Replaces: waiter --timeout (W1105), fleet.ceiling's wall-clock seconds (W1106), LOG.seconds as wall seconds. Keep those working until this lands. | 2026-10-13: 2026-10-13 DESIGN CORRECTION: RLIMIT_CPU is per process, and mikemol-commit's real work runs in other processes (bazel), so an rlimit on the waiter's child bounds almost nothing. The compliant mechanism is the absence witness: W1125 streams the child's output into its log, W1124 reads the CPU of the child's whole process tree from /proc, W1126 declares a hang only when the log has stopped growing AND the tree CPU has stopped advancing, then ends the child. This card removes W1105's --timeout and W1106's wall-seconds ceiling once W1126 lands, keeping at most one generous commented backstop. | 2026-10-15: all children done: W1124, W1125, W1126, W1130 (derived by --close-umbrellas dry run, d0fba6a)

waypoints.title: Gate ledger rows carry each check's CPU seconds, peak parallelism and the first line of its refusal, beside pass/fail; old rows still read
waypoints.evidence: 2026-10-13: 2026-10-13 operator request via github-8f: profile the pre-commit checks so they can be classified by cheapness for automatic runs from the harness (hooks at some minimum frequency) instead of work piling up behind commit checks and the commit aborting on a simple error. Properties: (1) CPU seconds per check, NEVER wall time (host chronically oversubscribed; operator rule: no wall-clock reliance, it makes synchronization nondeterministic), peak parallelism, refusal frequency, first-failure rank; (2) a histogram of 'refused because' by check from the ledger; (3) a Victoria series per check plus a dashboard, and a classification column; (4) a proposed, not decided, heuristic: a check under N CPU-seconds solo that catches at least M percent of aborts is a candidate for the edit hook, N and M derived from the ledger's distribution. DESIGN: the existing gate ledger (hooks/src/mikemol/hooks/gate_ledger.py, TSV: iso8601, gate, status, seconds) records WALL seconds, so the first step is the recorder: add CPU seconds (rusage children delta), peak parallelism and the first line of the refusal as extra columns; the reader treats a short row as an old row (cause unknown, CPU unknown), as it already skips short rows. Peak parallelism needs the check's concurrent children count; where it cannot be measured say so rather than write 0. Chain: W1115 recorder -> W1116 --profile -> W1117 Victoria series + dashboard (a luthen ask: the dashboard) and W1118 classification + heuristic. | 2026-10-13: 2026-10-13 luthen-observability-d9 asks for gate START and END epochs and host per row, to correlate RAPL package power with commit-gate runs (luthen W934/W932, read-only). So add to this card's columns: start_epoch, end_epoch (UTC seconds, integers, not local-time strings) and host, and wire mtools' own pre-commit to record per check.

pathsforward --block-behind-open: block each ready card behind its open enablers (local and repo:W<n>), idempotent, dry run without --write
waypoints.evidence: 2026-10-13: 2026-10-13 nemik:W476 (read in nemik's queue): ReadyBehindOpen (nemik:W465) flags a card stored ready or working while an open card enables it, for the case the umbrella rule (2+ own children) leaves out; fleet count 88, 55 of them paperkit W145-W200; mtools W1115-W1118 (behind W1122), W1019, W1100, W1128-W1130, W833. Design: a pure function over the State (blocked_on gets the open enablers, blocked_kind agent) in its own module, wired as an idempotent mode beside --prune-landed and --block-matching (W947 precedent: dry run without --write, then all-or-none). DECISIONS: (1) only READY cards are blocked; a WORKING card is being done by definition, so it is reported and left. (2) only OPEN enablers count (not done, not residue); a cross-repo enabler is read through the same foreign resolution as --prune-landed and written as repo:W<n>. (3) the existing prune returns the card to ready when the enabler lands, so no new unblock path. (4) The assumption to state in the output: it treats 'X enables Y' as 'Y waits for X'; an edge that is only a hint, not a prerequisite, should be dropped first (nemik's umbrella rule says the same). (5) a card that already has a blocked_on of its own keeps it and gains the enablers.

waypoints.title: mikemol-paths-forward mode that takes an operator ruling (the AskUserQuestion question and answer text, with its time) and lifts exactly the one held row it names, refusing every other change, so standing rule 5 holds against agents and not against the operator's own words

waypoints.evidence: 2026-10-15: 2026-10-15 DESIGN QUESTION before building (github-8f asked for W1194's distance): the mode takes ruling text from its caller and cannot verify the operator wrote it; an agent can type the same text, so a mode that lifts on recorded text moves rule 5's guard to whoever supplies the text. Options that hold against agents: (a) the operator runs the lift themselves in their own shell (the tool refuses when run by an agent session, by the env the harness sets); (b) the ruling is read from a file only the operator's side can write (a path outside the agent's write permission); (c) the lift needs a token the operator mints. Which is for the operator to choose; I have not picked one. Distance: not near until that is chosen; the code itself is one mode with a refuse-everything-else test. | 2026-10-15: 2026-10-15 OPERATOR DECISION, relayed by github-8f (not verified by this session): the lift is authorised by the operator's TOTP from their phone; the code does not lift the row itself but authorises OpenBao to SIGN the ruling payload (card, ruling text, time) with a non-exportable transit key (luthen-observability:W1075, read: it currently describes a TOTP validate-only policy, so its text predates the signing step and luthen has to carry it). The lift mode: builds the canonical payload, submits it with the code for signing, records payload plus signature, and changes exactly the named held row only when the signature verifies against the transit public key checked into the repo. Tests: a valid signature lifts that row only; a signature over a different card or ruling text refuses; no signature refuses; wrong or reused code is OpenBao's to refuse. Split here: W1270 the pure core with an injected verifier (buildable now); W1271 how signatures are verified inside a dependency-free package (stdlib has no ed25519/ecdsa verify: options are an external openssl, a dependency, or opa); the OpenBao signing call is blocked on luthen-observability:W1075. | 2026-10-15: mtools half BUILT: lift core 20f7106 and the command line 078a057 (--lift JWS --jwk FILE). Left: luthen-observability:W1075 (the OpenBao transit key, its public JWK to check in, the signing request path); nudged them with the three concrete needs. Once the JWK exists, the repo checks it in and the operator runs the signing request, then --lift. | 2026-10-15: 2026-10-15 luthen-observability-d9 (testimony): W1075 items 1-2 (transit ed25519 key exportable=false in terraform+Rego, public JWK from its public part, one-time raw-signature demonstration) are ready on luthen's side and do not wait on the operator; item 3, the request path, waits on the operator choosing (A) login MFA in front of a one-use sign-only token or (B) a broker. waypoints.title: Decide how the lift verifies an OpenBao transit signature without a new dependency in pathsforward
waypoints.evidence: 2026-10-15: 2026-10-15 RULING (github-8f, repo-level): reuse opa, the dependency pathsforward pins. CHOSEN ROUTE: opa. RAN (not from memory): opa 1.20.2 from the bazel cache; 'opa capabilities --current' lists io.jwt.verify_eddsa (and es256/384/512, rs, ps, hs); a probe script (a scratch Python file using openssl genpkey ed25519 to make a key, a compact JWS with header alg EdDSA and canonical payload {card, ruling, time}, signed with openssl pkeyutl -sign -rawin, the public key as a JWK {kty OKP, crv Ed25519, x = base64url of the raw 32 bytes}) evaluated io.jwt.verify_eddsa(JWS, JWK): valid JWS -> true; the same signature over a payload naming a different card -> false; empty signature -> false; 64 zero bytes -> false. So the lift can verify with opa and no new dependency, and the openssl fallback is not needed. NOT PROVEN HERE: that OpenBao's transit ed25519 sign over the exact JWS signing input (non-prehashed) yields a raw signature this verifier accepts, and the form of the transit public key; that is luthen-observability:W1075's to demonstrate with a real key, and W1270's verifier seam should take the JWK so either way works.

waypoints.title: pycodemod futureimport planner removes the annotations future import and quotes forward class names, listing unquotable bases
waypoints.evidence: 2026-10-16: 2026-10-16 DESIGN from reading pycodemod's orempty (planner plan(text)->Planned wrapped by cli_typedargs.print_judged, judged by the project's mypy+ruff so a rewrite lands only when findings do not rise). The future-import verb is the same shape: a libcst planner that removes the import line. Mypy does NOT see the failure that matters (an unquoted forward reference is fine to mypy and a NameError on 3.13 at import), so the planner must itself quote three classes of annotation name: (1) a class used before its module-level definition or inside its own body, (2) a name bound only under 'if TYPE_CHECKING:' (346 of 453 tree modules have the TYPE_CHECKING import, so this is the dominant case), (3) a name from a module that would become a runtime import cycle. Class 2 interacts with W1343: Codon rejects TYPE_CHECKING itself, so a quoted TYPE_CHECKING-only name is an interim form; the end state turns those into real imports, where cycles then decide. Atomized: W1326a planner for classes 1 and 3-free case, dry run lists the sites; W1326b the TYPE_CHECKING-bound case; both before any --write. | 2026-10-16: commit 65ac1e5 (pushed): futureimport.plan, 4 tests. waypoints.evidence: 2026-10-19: 2026-10-19 design finding from reading domain_witness.sh and the ratchet BUILD: the witness proves the BUILD GRAPH's domain, arm 1 that a content change to the victim reaches the //ratchet:mypy action, arm 2 that a planted transitive defect reaches its verdict. Arm 1 can be a static fact bazel already holds: bazel query 'victim intersect deps(//ratchet:mypy)' returned //ratchet:src/mikemol/ratchet/state.py (read-only, ran in the live workspace). So arm 1 becomes a genquery over deps(//ratchet:mypy) plus a py_test that asserts the victim label is in its output (cacheable, no nested bazel). Arm 2 becomes a py_test running the mypy runner directly over a sandboxed copy with the defect planted, expecting red, and over the unplanted copy expecting green (the control). The existing test loop in ratchet/BUILD.bazel globs tests/test_*.py into targets with no data, so the genquery test needs its own target with data = [the genquery]. New files: a test module and its warrants, no new root shell script (a root script would bring the shellcheck-registered and orphan checks). | 2026-10-20: landed 8f594d63

waypoints.evidence: 2026-10-20: 2026-10-20 readings (github-8f's three checks): (1) With --local_cpu_resources=7 and hooks shards declaring cpu:8, eight shards (hooks 1, 6, 12, pycodemod 0, 1, pathsforward 5, treeio 0, debtplan 0) were ALL executing at once (pgrep of their runner shells): bazel neither waited for 8 free cores nor serialised them, so the cpu:K tag is not reserving anything for these sh_test shards. The pool cap alone does not stop the oversubscription; the 31 timeouts need another edge, e.g. --local_test_jobs sized as free cores divided by the declared K, or a host-ledger lease per shard. Reading the outcome when the run ends. (2) The gate runs mikemol-gate-jobs through the live bazel-bin link, so this edit changes every gate before it has passed one: the W1743 class (bazel-bin of a live working tree is not a pinned tool). Acceptable tonight; W1743 stays near the top. (3) The pool, like --jobs, is sampled once at gate start from load1, a spot reading; bazel's pool does not follow load during the run. | 2026-10-20: 2026-10-20 second reading (github-8f: why cpu:K did not reserve): the macro is NOT at fault. bazel query on //hooks:mutants_1 shows tags = [cpu:8], env MUTATE_JOBS=8 and MUTATE_SHARD=1/24, size = medium: the tag is on the sh_test. Bazel's own help documents --local_resources as limiting concurrent actions by test tags of the form resources:NAME:AMOUNT, and mentions cpu:3 only as the sandbox LIMIT form (--experimental_sandbox_enforce_resources_regexp). So cpu:8 is likely not the scheduling reservation; resources:cpu:8 may be. To test: add resources:cpu:K beside cpu:K in the macro and rerun three hooks shards with a pool of 8, expecting one at a time. waypoints.title: Mutation runs are one bazel target per site in hierarchical BUILD files, so the cache skips every unchanged site
waypoints.next_bounded_step: Corrected by the operator (2026-10-22, real user turn): thousands of targets are fine when the build files are properly hierarchical, so go EXHAUSTIVE, not grouped: one target per mutation site, generated into one BUILD file per module package (a root file loads a macro, each module's file holds only its own sites), declared inputs the mutated module's source, the tests that reach it (importdag) and the runner, so editing a module reruns that module's sites and every other site hits the cache. No shard count, no hash, no balancing table: balance is each site's own cost. Risks to measure first, not assume: bazel analysis and per-target startup at thousands of targets, and the gate's per-target metric series (mikemol.gate.target.* carries a target label, so thousands of targets may exceed luthen's family ceiling: ask luthen-observability before the first run). Atomize: (1) measure per-site CPU and startup in the current runner, (2) importdag gives each module's reaching tests, (3) a generator writes the hierarchical BUILD files from the mutants.regex and the site finder (W1761 is its single site finder), (4) shardgate and the gate metrics are told sites are targets. Do not extend the flat 131.

waypoints.title: One landing record, the same for every repo, which nemik's landings.json and round sizing read
waypoints.next_bounded_step: Make the single-commit path (and the train and the refusal and withdrawal paths) call the same record builder as emit_stack, on every call, and test that a single commit produces the record with the final shape (event landing | refused | withdrawn, flat strings, card, cards, stack_key and stack_index when present, path, gate_s, verdict, reason, pushed, notes). Tell luthen-observability-ab and nemik-84 now that --ship will not do it. I still need the build, W1969
waypoints.evidence: 2026-10-25: 2026-10-25 FINDING (github-8f's lead, checked): on the single-commit path commit_kata.after_of ships the verdict lines (ship_text) ONLY when --ship is on the command line; spans are emitted either way. A search of every .py, .sh and .toml under ~/github for the flag finds it in mtools' own code and tests and in luthen's checks/land.py, where the hit is --ships-host (a different flag, the host-drift acknowledgement) and not --ship. So NO caller in the fleet passes --ship, and a repo that lands with single commits (luthen) writes no landing record, which is why nemik's landings file holds none of theirs. The stack path calls emit_stack unconditionally (commit_kata line 918); I have NOT verified that emit_stack writes the same landing event nemik reads, which is the first thing to check. Conclusion matches github-8f's: the landing record is written on every call and every path, never behind a flag | 2026-10-25: 2026-10-25 nemik-84 ANSWERS (read from src/nemik/landings.py and hostroot's reader): (1) the reader takes a landing's time from the log record's _time and ignores any body field, so landed_at is kept ONLY if a stack emits its records together after the gate; (2) derive the stack, do not send its size: key plus index suffices (stack = records sharing a key; the reader infers a stack today from a run of equal gate_s, a guess); keep size only if refused or withdrawn entries must count in it; (3) only landed counts toward round size, refused and withdrawn are kept and counted apart as PRESSURE (a refused gate costs gate_s), never as throughput. TRAP A: the reader accepts event == 'landing' only, so the landed kind keeps the word 'landing' (refused and withdrawn get their own words, e.g. 'refused', 'withdrawn'). TRAP B: the reader is hostroot's flat-JSON reader (strings and lists of strings, no nested objects, no booleans): emit stack as flat keys stack_key and stack_index (and stack_size only if needed), pushed as the text true or false; cards as a list of strings is fine. Nothing built on nemik's side until the record exists (nemik:W1042 blocked on github:W48) | 2026-10-25: 2026-10-25 CHECKED emit_stack: the stack path calls emit_landings(text, lease-to-verdict seconds, env) right after the stack's verdict (commit_span.emit_stack, W1738), so a stack's records are emitted together at its end; the stack lands in one fast-forward step, so that instant IS the landing within seconds and landed_at adds nothing (nemik reads _time). luthen-observability-ab: land.py never passed --ship (their W1636 adds it); asks for the primary card (--waypoint) beside cards, and a free place for pre-steps to put per-repo facts (their HOST ROWS). FINAL SHAPE, flat for hostroot's reader (strings and lists of strings only): event = landing | refused | withdrawn (landed keeps the word 'landing'); repo; sha; subject; card (the primary, --waypoint); cards (list of every Waypoint trailer symbol); stack_key and stack_index (strings, absent for a direct landing); path = direct | stack | train; gate_s; verdict = pass | refused | withdrawn; reason (refused and withdrawn only); pushed = 'true' | 'false'; notes (list of 'key=value' strings the declared pre-steps print on lines beginning NOTE, so host_rows rides as 'host_rows=2' with no luthen-specific field in mikemol-commit) | 2026-10-25: 2026-10-25 CORRECTION OF MY OWN EARLIER FINDING, from reading both writers. I said the single-commit path writes no landing record unless --ship is passed. WRONG IN ONE WAY THAT MATTERS: there are two different writers. (a) --ship goes through verdictlog.ship_text then ship_events, which spools the run's VERDICT events (event_of and gate_event_of lines, their own shape) for a detached drainer; (b) the 'landing' record nemik reads (event landing, repo, sha, card, gate_s, pushed, verdict) is made ONLY by commit_span.landing_records and shipped by commit_span.emit_landings, whose single caller in the package is emit_stack (commit_span.py line 373), the STACK path. So a single commit never writes a landing record, with or without --ship, and luthen's W1636 (adding --ship to checks/land.py) will NOT make nemik see its landings. The fix is the card itself: one landing record written by every path

waypoints.title: A train leader that started before a stack was submitted leaves it for the next leader, so measure how often that is and what it costs
waypoints.next_bounded_step: Measure from the landing spans: for the last day, how many stacks were submitted after the leader's lease and how long each waited for the next leader; then decide whether to do nothing, to delay a leader's start by a no-progress witness, or to let a stack submit hold the lease until a declared burst ends. waypoints.evidence: 2026-10-25: 2026-10-25 WHY THE TRAIN DID NOT JOIN (github-8f's question, read from trainlead.lead): lead finds its followers ONCE, at the moment it takes the lease (_behind then trainjoin.followers over the queued keys then), and only stacks with a LARGER submit key and both ledger files (snap and items) join. W1953 began its gate before the later stacks (w1918c, w1954a, w1948c, w1961a, w1957) were submitted, so none could be joined, and a leader does not rescan mid-gate (the gate tests ONE tip, so a follower cannot join a run already underway). They are not lost: when W1953 ends, the next in submit order takes the lease and joins every stack behind it that is queued by then, which is all four. So the cost is one full gate for the leader plus a wait, not one gate each. What is open is how often followers arrive after a leader starts and how long that waits (the late-submit case), and whether a leader about to start can wait a short, CPU-bounded moment for stacks submitted in the same burst
